lessons.title: Design a Claude Project that keeps every answer on-brand
lessons.summary: Build a Claude Project with custom instructions and knowledge files so that every new chat writes in your voice, follows your rules, and knows your business without re-explaining anything.
lessons.goal: Create a reusable Claude Project whose custom instructions and knowledge files make every answer sound like your brand by default.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most professionals waste the first five messages of every chat re-explaining who they are, who their audience is, and how they want things written. Claude Projects (available on Pro and up) solve this: you define custom instructions and upload reference files once, and every new chat inside the project starts with that context loaded. The difference between generic AI output and on-brand output is almost entirely in this setup work, and it compounds across every future conversation.
lessons.beforeYouStart: You need a Claude Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan (Projects are not on the Free tier). Gather 2-4 examples of your best existing content and any brand or style guidelines you have.
steps: Collect your raw material: 2-4 samples of writing you consider perfectly on-brand, a short description of your audience, and any hard rules (banned words, legal disclaimers, formatting standards).
In Claude, create a new Project and give it a specific name like 'Acme — Client Communications', not just 'Work'.
Open the project's custom instructions and paste in a structured instruction block: who you are, who the audience is, voice rules, formatting rules, and things Claude must never do.
Upload your sample documents to the project knowledge so Claude can imitate real examples instead of guessing from adjectives like 'friendly'.

Start a new chat inside the project and give it a deliberately vague request like 'Write a short update email about the delayed shipment'. Vague requests reveal whether the instructions carry the weight.
Compare the output to your samples. Where it drifts, do not correct the chat — update the custom instructions, because chat-level fixes are lost but instruction-level fixes are permanent.
Repeat the vague-request test until output needs only light edits, then start using the project for real work.
lessons.prompt:
You are the writing assistant for [COMPANY NAME], a [ONE-LINE DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS].

AUDIENCE
We write for [PRIMARY AUDIENCE, e.g. "mid-market CFOs evaluating software"]. Assume they are busy, skeptical, and allergic to hype.

VOICE
- Tone: [e.g. "confident, plain-spoken, lightly warm — never salesy"]
- Sentences: mostly short. Vary rhythm. No filler openers like "In today's fast-paced world".
- We say "[PREFERRED TERM]", never "[BANNED TERM]".
- Match the style of the sample documents in this project's knowledge. When in doubt, imitate the samples over these adjectives.

HARD RULES
1. Never invent product features, prices, statistics, or customer names. If a fact is not in the project knowledge or my message, ask me instead of guessing.
2. Always include [REQUIRED ELEMENT, e.g. "a single clear call to action"] in customer-facing copy.
3. Never use: [LIST BANNED WORDS/PHRASES, e.g. "synergy, game-changing, unlock"].
4. Default lengths: emails under 150 words, social posts under 80 words, unless I say otherwise.

WORKFLOW
When I give you a task, first state in one line who the audience is and what the goal of the piece is, then write the draft. If my request is ambiguous, ask at most 2 clarifying questions before drafting.
lessons.explanation: This instruction block works because it separates identity, audience, voice, hard rules, and workflow into labeled sections that Claude can apply consistently. The 'imitate the samples over these adjectives' line is the key move: uploaded examples define tone far more precisely than descriptive words ever can. The anti-invention rule ('ask me instead of guessing') is your guardrail against Claude confidently fabricating a price or feature in customer-facing copy. Finally, the one-line audience-and-goal restatement forces Claude to show its interpretation before writing, so misunderstandings surface in one line instead of in a full wrong draft.
lessons.example:
A boutique accounting firm creates a project called 'Firm — Client Emails'. Custom instructions define the audience (small-business owners who fear tax jargon), the voice (calm, plain-English, zero jargon without a translation), and hard rules (never give a definitive tax ruling; always recommend a call for edge cases). They upload three of the partner's best client emails.

Test prompt in a new project chat: 'Write an email telling clients about the new quarterly filing deadline.'

Result: instead of a generic corporate announcement, Claude produces a 120-word email that opens the way the partner does ('Quick heads-up so nothing sneaks up on you'), translates the regulation into one plain sentence, ends with the firm's standard 'book 15 minutes' call to action, and adds no invented details about the regulation.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, create a project for one recurring writing task in your work. Write custom instructions using the template above, upload at least two real examples of your best output, then test with a deliberately vague one-line request. Fix any drift by editing the instructions — not the chat — and test again.
lessons.expectedResult: A vague one-line request inside the project produces a draft that sounds recognizably like your samples, respects your hard rules, and needs only minor edits — with no re-explaining of context.
commonMistakes: Describing voice only with adjectives ('professional but friendly') and uploading no examples — Claude interprets adjectives generically; samples are what actually pin down tone.
Fixing style problems inside individual chats instead of updating the project instructions, so every new chat repeats the same drift.
Writing one mega-project for everything. A project scoped to 'client emails' outperforms a vague 'my company' project because the instructions can be specific.
Leaving out anti-invention rules, then discovering Claude confidently made up a product detail in copy that went to a customer.
lessons.proTip: Add a final instruction: 'End every draft with a one-line note listing any facts I should verify before sending.' You get a built-in fact-check reminder attached to every piece of copy the project produces.

lessons.title: Compare, reconcile and synthesize multiple documents in one pass
lessons.summary: Upload several related files to Claude and get a structured comparison: what agrees, what conflicts, what is missing, and one synthesized answer you can act on.
lessons.goal: Turn a pile of overlapping documents into a single reconciliation table and a synthesized summary, with every claim traced back to its source file.
lessons.whyItMatters: Real work rarely lives in one document: you get three vendor proposals, two versions of a contract, or five sets of interview notes, and someone has to find where they agree and where they quietly contradict each other. Doing this by hand is slow and error-prone. Claude accepts up to 20 files per chat (30 MB each — PDFs, Word, Excel, CSV, text), and with the right prompt it will cross-reference them systematically instead of summarizing each one in isolation.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have 2-4 related documents ready that genuinely overlap in subject — comparison prompts are wasted on unrelated files.
steps: Choose documents that answer the same underlying question, such as three supplier quotes or two contract drafts, and upload them all to one chat.
Name each file in your prompt exactly as uploaded, and state the decision the comparison must support — 'which supplier to pick', not just 'compare these'.
Ask for three explicit sections: agreements, conflicts, and gaps (things at least one document covers that others are silent on).
Require source attribution: every claim must name the document it came from, and conflicts must quote or closely paraphrase both sides.
Ask a follow-up question about the point that matters most to your decision, and request the exact passage from each document that addresses it.
Spot-check two or three attributed claims against the originals before relying on the analysis — you own the final accuracy.
Ask for a one-paragraph synthesis and a recommendation only after the reconciliation table looks correct.
lessons.prompt:
I have uploaded [N] documents: [FILE 1 NAME], [FILE 2 NAME], [FILE 3 NAME]. They all relate to [TOPIC], and I need to decide [DECISION].

Analyze them together, not one by one. Produce:

1. AGREEMENTS — a bullet list of points where the documents are consistent. Name every document that supports each point.
2. CONFLICTS — a table with columns: Topic | What [FILE 1] says | What [FILE 2] says | What [FILE 3] says | Severity for my decision (high/medium/low). Quote or closely paraphrase the actual wording; do not smooth over differences.
3. GAPS — points that at least one document addresses while the others are silent. Silence is not agreement; flag it.
4. SYNTHESIS — one paragraph combining the documents into the best-supported overall picture, followed by a recommendation for [DECISION] with your reasoning.

Rules: use only what is actually in these documents — no outside knowledge and no invented details. Attribute every claim to its source document. If wording is ambiguous, say so rather than picking an interpretation silently.
lessons.explanation: The prompt's structure forces cross-referencing: by demanding agreements, conflicts, and gaps as separate sections, you prevent the common failure where Claude writes three polite standalone summaries. The conflicts table with quoted wording is the highest-value part — smoothed-over contradictions are exactly what get professionals in trouble. 'Silence is not agreement' catches the subtle case where one contract has a clause the other omits. Attribution plus the no-outside-knowledge rule makes every line checkable, which turns the output from an opinion into an audit trail; and holding the recommendation until section 4 keeps the analysis from being written backwards to justify a premature conclusion.
lessons.example:
An operations manager uploads three courier proposals: FastShip.pdf, RegionalExpress.pdf, and NorthCargo.pdf, asking which to shortlist for a national contract.

Claude's conflicts table surfaces that FastShip quotes '99.2% on-time delivery (metro areas)' while its rural coverage appears only in an appendix at 91%; RegionalExpress quotes a flat 96% nationwide. The gaps section flags that only NorthCargo mentions liability insurance limits at all — the other two are silent, which the manager had not noticed. The synthesis recommends shortlisting RegionalExpress and NorthCargo, and asking FastShip to restate rural performance before proceeding.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, upload two or three real overlapping documents from your work — proposals, policy versions, meeting notes on the same project — and run the prompt with a real decision filled in. Then verify one 'conflict' row against the original files.
lessons.expectedResult: A reconciliation with at least one conflict or gap you had not consciously registered, where every claim names its source document and the recommendation follows from the table rather than preceding it.
commonMistakes: Asking 'summarize these files' and getting sequential summaries with no cross-referencing — the comparison structure must be in your prompt.
Skipping attribution requirements, which makes the output impossible to verify and easy to trust blindly.
Uploading documents that don't actually overlap, then blaming the model for a thin comparison.
Accepting the synthesis without spot-checking any quoted conflicts — Claude is strong at this task but you remain responsible for accuracy on decisions that matter.
lessons.proTip: For recurring comparisons (monthly vendor reviews, contract redlines), save this prompt structure in a Project so the reconciliation format is applied automatically every time.

lessons.title: Build interactive documents and small tools with Claude Artifacts
lessons.summary: Use Artifacts to turn a conversation into a polished, self-contained deliverable — an interactive checklist, a calculator, a one-page site — that renders live next to the chat and can be shared.
lessons.goal: Produce a working interactive artifact — a small web tool or polished document — through iterative refinement, and share it with someone else.
lessons.whyItMatters: Artifacts move Claude's output out of the chat bubble and into a live side panel: documents, diagrams, code, and fully interactive web apps or React components you can actually click. That changes what 'asking Claude for help' can produce — instead of instructions for a pricing calculator, you get the calculator. Since June 2026 you can also edit an artifact in place by highlighting a section and typing the change, and artifacts can be published and shared, which makes them genuine deliverables for clients and colleagues, not just previews.
steps: Pick something interactive or standalone: a quote calculator, an onboarding checklist that tracks completion, a one-page explainer. Plain prose questions won't trigger an artifact — buildable things do.
Describe the tool like a mini product brief: who uses it, what inputs it takes, what it computes or displays, and roughly how it should look. Explicitly say 'build this as an interactive artifact'.
Test the first version in the preview panel by actually using it — enter realistic values, click everything, try an edge case like zero or a huge number.

Request changes in small batches referring to what you see: 'the total ignores the discount field' beats 'improve it'. For small text tweaks, highlight the section in the artifact and type the change directly.
Put real business logic in explicitly — exact rates, thresholds, wording — because Claude will otherwise fill gaps with plausible invented numbers.
When it works, ask for finishing touches: your company name, sensible defaults, a short instruction line at the top for first-time users.
Publish or share the artifact so a colleague can try it, and note their first point of confusion — that is your next iteration.
lessons.prompt:
Build an interactive artifact: a [TOOL TYPE, e.g. "project quote calculator"] for [WHO WILL USE IT, e.g. "my freelance clients"].

Inputs:
- [INPUT 1, e.g. "Number of pages (1-50)"]
- [INPUT 2, e.g. "Design complexity: basic / standard / premium"]
- [INPUT 3, e.g. "Rush delivery: yes/no"]

Logic (use these exact numbers, do not invent your own):
- [RULE 1, e.g. "Base price 120 EUR per page"]
- [RULE 2, e.g. "Complexity multiplier: basic x1, standard x1.4, premium x1.9"]
- [RULE 3, e.g. "Rush adds 25% to the total"]

Output: show a clear itemized breakdown and a large final total that updates as inputs change.

Design: clean and professional, works on mobile, [BRAND COLOR] as the accent color, with a one-line explanation at the top telling users what this tool does. Handle silly inputs gracefully (empty fields, out-of-range numbers) instead of showing errors or NaN.
lessons.explanation: This works because it is structured like a product brief: inputs, logic, output, and design are separated, so nothing important is left for Claude to guess. The 'use these exact numbers' line is critical — business logic is the one place where a plausible-looking invention (a made-up multiplier) silently corrupts the tool. Naming the audience shapes tone and labeling choices; a client-facing calculator gets different wording than an internal one. The graceful-input requirement anticipates the most common flaw in first-draft tools, and asking for an itemized breakdown rather than just a total makes the tool's logic inspectable, so you can verify the math before anyone else uses it.
lessons.example:
A photographer asks for a session quote calculator: inputs for session type (portrait/wedding/commercial), hours, and travel distance; her real price list pasted into the logic section; her studio's dark green as the accent.

First version looks right but charges travel from kilometer zero. She replies: 'First 30 km should be free — only charge 0.60 EUR/km beyond that.' Claude updates the artifact in place. She then highlights the heading, types her studio name, tests with a 200-km wedding booking against her own manual calculation, and shares the published link. Clients now self-quote before the first call, and calls start from real budgets.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, build one small tool you would genuinely use this month — a price estimator, a decision checklist, an event countdown page. Use the brief structure above with your real numbers, test at least one edge case, and make one in-place edit by highlighting text in the artifact.
lessons.expectedResult: A working interactive artifact whose calculations match your real business rules, which survives an edge-case test, and which you could share with a colleague or client as-is.
commonMistakes: Vague briefs like 'make me a pricing tool' — Claude invents plausible rates and structure, and you spend more time un-guessing than you saved.
Judging the artifact by its looks without testing the logic; polished styling routinely hides a broken discount rule.
Requesting ten changes in one message, then being unable to tell which change broke the layout — batch 2-3 changes at a time.
Rebuilding from scratch in a new chat when one feature misbehaves, instead of iterating on the existing artifact where all your refinements live.
lessons.proTip: Ask Claude to add a visible version note ('v3 — updated travel rules') inside the artifact. When you iterate over several sessions or share updated links, everyone can tell at a glance which version they're using.

lessons.title: Package a repeatable workflow as a Claude Skill
lessons.summary: Turn a process you repeat every week into a Claude Skill — a reusable instruction package Claude loads automatically whenever the task comes up.
lessons.goal: Create a custom Claude Skill that encodes one repeatable expert workflow, so Claude performs it your way every time without re-prompting.
lessons.whyItMatters: Claude Skills (launched October 2025, expanded with Skills 2.0 in early 2026) are modular folders — a SKILL.md instruction file plus optional scripts and reference assets — that Claude loads on demand when a task matches. Anthropic ships pre-built skills for Excel, PowerPoint, Word, and PDF files, and you can create custom ones that work across Claude.ai, Claude Code, and the API. The professional payoff: instead of pasting the same 400-word mega-prompt every Monday, you encode the procedure once, and it becomes something your whole team can reuse. The format is even an open standard (agentskills.io).
lessons.beforeYouStart: Check that Skills and custom skill creation are enabled in your Claude account's settings (Settings → Capabilities on paid plans). Pick a workflow you have already done manually with Claude at least twice — skills encode proven processes, not hopes.
steps: Choose one recurring, well-defined workflow with a clear trigger and output — 'turn a signed proposal into a project kickoff checklist', not 'help with projects'.
Write down how you actually do it today: the steps, the rules you apply, the format of the finished product, and 1-2 examples of good output.
Draft the skill as a SKILL.md: a name, a one-line description of when the skill applies (this is what Claude matches against), then the procedure, rules, and an output template.
Make the description trigger-precise: 'Use when the user asks to convert meeting notes into a client status update' — vague descriptions mean the skill fires never or always.
Create the skill in your Claude account (via skill settings or by asking Claude itself to help you draft the SKILL.md from your written procedure).
Test with a real input phrased naturally, the way you'd ask on a busy day — confirm the skill activates and the output follows your template.
Fix failures at the right layer: activation problems mean the description needs sharper trigger language; output problems mean the procedure or template needs tightening.
Share the skill with your team once it is reliable, so the process stops living only in your head.
lessons.prompt:
Help me package a workflow as a Claude Skill. Draft the full SKILL.md.

Workflow name: [NAME, e.g. "Client status update from raw notes"]
Trigger: this skill applies when [PRECISE TRIGGER, e.g. "I ask to turn project notes or a work log into a client-facing status update"].

My current manual process:
[DESCRIBE YOUR STEPS, e.g. "1. Pull out completed items, in-progress items, and blockers. 2. Rewrite in client-friendly language — no internal jargon or team-member blame. 3. Add a 'what we need from you' section if anything is waiting on the client. 4. Keep it under 250 words."]

Hard rules:
- [RULE 1, e.g. "Never mention internal staffing issues"]
- [RULE 2, e.g. "Every blocker must state what unblocks it"]

Here is one example of a finished output I consider excellent:
[PASTE EXAMPLE]

Write the SKILL.md with: (1) a name and a one-line description optimized so Claude reliably recognizes when to apply this skill, (2) the step-by-step procedure, (3) the hard rules, (4) the output template derived from my example. Then tell me one likely failure mode of this skill and how to phrase the description to avoid it.
lessons.explanation: This prompt has Claude do the packaging while you supply the expertise — the division of labor that makes skills good. Your manual process and example output are the load-bearing content: a skill built from a vague wish produces vague results, while one built from a proven procedure inherits its quality. The emphasis on the one-line description reflects how skills actually work: Claude decides whether to load a skill by matching your request against that description, making it the single highest-leverage sentence in the file. Asking for a likely failure mode up front turns your first test run from a blind trial into a targeted check.
lessons.example:
A recruiter turns her candidate-screening summary process into a skill. Trigger: 'when I paste interview notes and ask for a screening summary'. Procedure: extract experience relevant to the role's must-haves, flag gaps honestly, score communication from evidence in the notes only, output a five-section template ending with advance/hold/reject and reasoning. Hard rule: never infer anything about protected characteristics; base every judgment on stated evidence.

Before: pasting a 350-word prompt from a notes app for every candidate, with drifting formats. After: she pastes notes and types 'screening summary for the backend role' — the skill activates, and every summary lands in the same comparable format her hiring managers now expect.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, pick one task you have prompted for at least twice in the past month. Run the prompt above with your real procedure and a real example, create the skill from the drafted SKILL.md, then test it with a naturally phrased request and one input that should NOT trigger it.
lessons.expectedResult: The skill activates on a natural phrasing of the target task, stays silent on the unrelated request, and produces output matching your template — with no mega-prompt pasted.
commonMistakes: Building a skill for a process you haven't stabilized manually first — you end up encoding guesses and then debugging both the process and the packaging at once.
Writing a broad description like 'helps with client communication', so the skill triggers on everything or nothing.
Omitting a concrete example output, leaving the template underspecified and the results inconsistent — the exact problem skills exist to solve.
Cramming three workflows into one skill; three small skills with precise triggers beat one bloated one.
lessons.proTip: Version your skills: keep a 'Changelog' line at the bottom of SKILL.md noting what changed and when. When a teammate reports odd output, you can immediately connect it to the last edit.

lessons.title: Run deep research with a structured brief instead of a question
lessons.summary: Replace one-line research questions with a structured research brief that defines scope, sources, deliverable format and confidence labels — and get research you can actually defend.
lessons.goal: Write a structured research brief that directs Claude's web-search-backed research toward a decision-ready, source-cited deliverable.
lessons.whyItMatters: Claude has built-in web search with citations and decides when to search, which makes it a genuine research assistant — but the difference between 'interesting reading' and 'research I can take into a meeting' is the brief. Professionals who hand analysts a scope, key questions, and a deliverable format get usable work back; the same discipline applies to Claude. A structured brief also creates natural checkpoints, so you catch a wrong direction after the outline instead of after twenty minutes of reading.
steps: Write down the decision the research serves and what would change your mind — research without a decision attached becomes an unfocused reading list.
Draft the brief: context, 3-5 specific key questions, explicit scope boundaries (time period, geography, what to ignore), and source preferences.
Define the deliverable precisely: sections, rough length, and a requirement that every factual claim carries a citation.
Require confidence labels — well-established / single-source / uncertain — so you can see where the ground is firm before you lean on it.
Send the brief and ask for a research plan first: which questions Claude will tackle in what order, and what it expects to be hardest to source. Correct course here, cheaply.
Approve the plan, then review the deliverable question by question against the brief rather than reading it like an article.
Click through the citations on the 2-3 claims your decision most depends on, then ask follow-ups where evidence was thin.
lessons.prompt:
I need you to research a topic for a real decision. Use web search and cite sources throughout.

CONTEXT: [WHO YOU ARE AND THE SITUATION, e.g. "I run a 12-person design agency considering opening a second office"].
DECISION THIS SUPPORTS: [DECISION, e.g. "choose between Lisbon and Valencia by end of month"].

KEY QUESTIONS (address each separately):
1. [QUESTION 1]
2. [QUESTION 2]
3. [QUESTION 3]

SCOPE: Focus on [TIME PERIOD, e.g. "2024 or newer data"] and [GEOGRAPHY/SEGMENT]. Explicitly ignore [OUT OF SCOPE, e.g. "remote-only setups"].
SOURCES: Prefer [e.g. "official statistics, government portals, established business press"]. Treat vendor marketing content and forums as weak evidence and label them as such.

DELIVERABLE: A report with (a) a 5-bullet executive summary, (b) one section per key question with citations for every factual claim, (c) a comparison table if the questions involve options, (d) a 'What I could not verify' section listing gaps and conflicting sources.

Label each major finding: WELL-ESTABLISHED (multiple independent sources), SINGLE-SOURCE, or UNCERTAIN (conflicting or thin evidence).

Before researching, show me your research plan in 5 lines or fewer and wait for my go-ahead.
lessons.explanation: Each section of the brief closes a specific failure mode. Naming the decision keeps every search anchored to relevance. Numbered key questions convert one fuzzy topic into checkable sub-deliverables. Scope boundaries and source preferences prevent the classic drift into outdated data and vendor marketing dressed up as fact. The confidence labels are the professional-grade element — they transform the report from uniform-sounding prose into a map of strong and weak ground — and the 'What I could not verify' section legitimizes honesty about gaps, counteracting the tendency to paper over missing evidence. The plan-first checkpoint costs one message and routinely saves the whole run.
lessons.example:
A financial analyst uses the brief to evaluate whether a client should enter the refurbished-electronics market. Key questions cover market size and growth, top competitors' positioning, and regulatory obligations for refurbished goods sold in the EU. Scope excludes the US market; sources prefer Eurostat, industry associations, and filings.

The research plan comes back proposing to lead with the regulatory question since it could kill the idea outright — a sequencing the analyst approves. The final report labels market-size figures WELL-ESTABLISHED across three sources, flags one competitor's claimed growth as SINGLE-SOURCE (their own press release), and the 'could not verify' section notes that pending EU right-to-repair changes may alter warranty obligations. The analyst clicks through the regulatory citations, then forwards the report with two sentences of her own judgment on top.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, write a full research brief for one question your work actually faces this quarter. Include all sections — context, decision, key questions, scope, sources, deliverable, confidence labels — request the plan first, and verify the citations behind the two findings your decision most depends on.
lessons.expectedResult: A cited, confidence-labeled report organized around your key questions, at least one finding marked single-source or uncertain, and a plan checkpoint that let you steer before the research ran.
commonMistakes: Asking a one-line question ('research the refurbished electronics market') and receiving a generic overview aimed at no decision.
Skipping confidence labels, so a claim sourced from one press release reads as authoritative as one confirmed by three official sources.
Treating citations as decoration — never clicking any — and repeating an error in a meeting where someone else checks.
Omitting scope boundaries, then getting research that is half about markets or time periods you don't care about.
lessons.proTip: Save your brief as a template in a Project with the structure fixed and blanks for context and questions. Your research quality stops depending on how carefully you prompt on a busy day.

lessons.title: Advanced prompting: examples, step-wise reasoning and output contracts
lessons.summary: Combine three intermediate prompting techniques — worked examples, explicit reasoning steps, and a strict output contract — to make Claude's answers consistent enough to build workflows on.
lessons.goal: Write a prompt that uses an example, a mandated reasoning order, and a fixed output format to produce consistent, verifiable results across many inputs.
lessons.whyItMatters: Beginner prompting gets you good one-off answers; professional workflows need consistent answers — the tenth invoice processed like the first, every candidate summary in the same format. Three techniques deliver that consistency: examples show instead of describe (one worked example outperforms three paragraphs of description), step-wise reasoning instructions control the order Claude works through a problem so it evaluates before concluding, and an output contract pins the response format so results are comparable and even machine-readable. These are the same principles Anthropic's own prompting guidance teaches, and they compound when combined.
steps: Identify a task you run repeatedly where output consistency matters — triaging requests, scoring leads, classifying feedback, extracting terms from documents.
Write the task instruction plainly, then add one fully worked example: a realistic input and exactly the output you want for it, formatted precisely how you want every future output.
Add a reasoning order: number the steps Claude must work through before answering — 'first identify X, then check Y against Z, then and only then classify'.
Define the output contract: the exact fields or sections, allowed values for each ('severity must be exactly one of: low, medium, high'), and what to output when information is missing.
Ban improvisation explicitly: no extra fields, no commentary outside the contract, missing data marked as specified rather than guessed.
Test on three inputs: a typical case, an edge case, and one with missing information. Compare outputs field by field.
Fix inconsistencies by tightening the contract or upgrading the example — if outputs drift in the same way twice, your example probably demonstrates the drift.
lessons.prompt:
You triage incoming [ITEM TYPE, e.g. "customer support requests"] for [CONTEXT, e.g. "a B2B software company"].

REASONING ORDER — work through these steps in order before answering:
1. Identify what the person is actually asking for, beneath how they phrased it.
2. Check for signals of [KEY RISK, e.g. "churn risk: mentions of cancelling, competitors, or repeated unresolved issues"].
3. Determine which team owns this: [TEAM A / TEAM B / TEAM C].
4. Only then assign severity.

OUTPUT CONTRACT — respond with exactly these fields and nothing else:
SUMMARY: one sentence, max 20 words
TEAM: exactly one of [TEAM A, TEAM B, TEAM C]
SEVERITY: exactly one of low, medium, high
CHURN_RISK: yes or no, plus a quoted phrase from the message as evidence, or "no — no signals present"
SUGGESTED_FIRST_REPLY: two sentences max

If information needed for a field is missing, write "UNKNOWN — needs human review" for that field. Never guess. Never add fields or commentary.

EXAMPLE
Input: "Third time writing about the export bug. If this isn't fixed this week we're moving to [Competitor]. Also, how do I add a new user seat?"
Output:
SUMMARY: Repeated unresolved export bug plus a routine seat-addition question.
TEAM: TEAM A
SEVERITY: high
CHURN_RISK: yes — "we're moving to [Competitor]"
SUGGESTED_FIRST_REPLY: We're escalating your export issue to a senior engineer today and will update you within 24 hours. I've also sent instructions for adding a user seat.

Now process this input:
[PASTE INPUT]
lessons.explanation: The three techniques close each other's gaps. The reasoning order makes Claude detect the churn signal and identify the real request before assigning severity — without it, severity gets decided first from surface tone and rationalized afterward. The output contract with enumerated values ('exactly one of') eliminates format drift, which is what makes outputs comparable across a hundred requests or parseable by another tool. The worked example resolves every ambiguity the instructions leave — note how it demonstrates the two-questions-in-one-message case, teaching more than a paragraph of rules would. The missing-data rule is the anti-hallucination guardrail: without a defined 'UNKNOWN' behavior, Claude fills gaps with plausible guesses.
lessons.example:
A sales manager adapts the template to score inbound leads: reasoning order (identify company size and need first, check budget signals, then score), a contract with SCORE 1-5, FIT_REASON, and NEXT_ACTION fields, and one worked example of a well-scored lead.

Before: 'What do you think of this lead?' produced thoughtful but structurally different answers every time — impossible to compare across a week of leads. After: forty leads through the template produce forty identical-format cards. Sorting by SCORE now takes seconds, and when one lead scores oddly, the FIT_REASON field shows exactly which reasoning step went wrong — fixable by tightening that step's instruction.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, build a triage or scoring prompt for a repetitive task in your work using all three techniques: one worked example, a numbered reasoning order, and an output contract with at least one enumerated field and a missing-data rule. Run it on three real inputs, including one with information missing.
lessons.expectedResult: Three outputs with identical structure and field names, correct enumerated values, and 'UNKNOWN — needs human review' where data was genuinely missing rather than a guess.
commonMistakes: Describing the desired format in prose instead of showing it — a worked example is worth more than any description of one.
Leaving field values open-ended ('rate the severity') so you get 'fairly high', '7/10', and 'significant' across three runs.
Providing an example that contradicts the written rules — Claude tends to follow the example, and you debug the wrong thing.
No missing-data rule, so gaps get filled with confident guesses that look exactly like real extractions.
lessons.proTip: For edge-case-heavy tasks, use two contrasting examples: one typical case and one tricky case handled correctly. The pair teaches the boundary between them better than either alone.

lessons.title: Turn meeting notes and transcripts into decisions, actions and follow-ups
lessons.summary: Feed raw meeting notes or a transcript to Claude and extract a clean record: decisions made, action items with owners and deadlines, open questions, and ready-to-send follow-up messages.
lessons.goal: Convert a messy transcript or set of notes into a structured meeting record and drafted follow-ups, with unclear ownership flagged instead of guessed.
lessons.whyItMatters: Meetings produce decisions and commitments that die in nobody's notes. The expensive failure is not a missing summary — it is the action item with no owner, or the 'decision' half the room remembers differently. Claude handles long transcripts easily (paste directly or upload the file), but the value comes from extraction discipline: separating what was decided from what was merely discussed, and refusing to invent owners or deadlines that were never actually said. Done well, this turns fifteen minutes of post-meeting admin into two.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have real notes or a transcript from a recent meeting. Auto-generated transcripts with speaker labels work well; rough personal notes work too — just tell Claude which kind it is getting.
steps: Paste or upload the raw material and state what kind it is: verbatim transcript with speaker labels, or your own compressed notes (Claude should treat inferences from rough notes more cautiously).
Give context the text lacks: meeting purpose, attendees and roles, and any decisions that were supposed to be made.
Ask for four separate sections — decisions, action items, open questions, and notable context — with a strict rule against mixing them.
Require every action item to have an owner and deadline from the text, with missing ones marked 'UNASSIGNED' or 'NO DEADLINE' rather than filled in plausibly.
Require evidence: each decision and action must reference the part of the conversation it came from, so anything surprising can be checked against the source.
Review the flagged gaps — those unassigned items are precisely the ones that would have fallen through the cracks — and resolve them yourself.
Ask for the follow-ups: a summary message for attendees and, if useful, individual reminders per action owner.
lessons.prompt:
Below are ["a verbatim transcript with speaker labels" / "my own rough notes"] from a meeting.

Context: [PURPOSE, e.g. "weekly project sync for the website relaunch"]. Attendees: [NAMES AND ROLES]. 

Extract the following, keeping the categories strictly separate:

1. DECISIONS MADE — only things actually decided, not topics discussed or leaning-towards. For each: the decision, who confirmed it, and a short quote or reference showing where it was made.
2. ACTION ITEMS — a table: Action | Owner | Deadline | Source in conversation. Use only owners and deadlines stated in the text. If an owner or deadline was never stated, write UNASSIGNED or NO DEADLINE — do not infer one, even when it seems obvious.
3. OPEN QUESTIONS — raised but not resolved, each with who raised it.
4. NOTABLE CONTEXT — risks, concerns, or constraints mentioned that don't fit above. Max 5 bullets.

Then list anything ambiguous — for example, discussion that might or might not have been a decision — under NEEDS CLARIFICATION rather than forcing it into a category.

Finally, draft a follow-up message to all attendees (under 200 words, neutral professional tone) summarizing decisions and actions, explicitly listing the UNASSIGNED items as needing owners.

[PASTE TRANSCRIPT OR NOTES]
lessons.explanation: The strict category separation attacks the core failure of meeting summaries: blending 'we discussed maybe doing X' into 'we decided X'. Requiring a quote or reference for each decision makes the record auditable — anyone who remembers differently checks the source, not their memory. The UNASSIGNED rule is deliberately counterintuitive: it forbids the obvious-seeming inference ('Maria talked about the design, so it's hers') because plausible auto-assignment is exactly how work slips through — Maria never agreed, and everyone assumed she had it. NEEDS CLARIFICATION gives genuinely ambiguous moments a home, so they surface for a human call instead of being silently forced into a category. The follow-up draft that names unassigned items turns the record into a mechanism that closes its own gaps.
lessons.example:
A project manager pastes a 40-minute relaunch-sync transcript. Claude extracts three decisions (including 'launch moves to Oct 12 — confirmed by Elena after the QA discussion' with the supporting quote), six action items — two marked UNASSIGNED, including 'update the pricing page copy', which everyone discussed and no one took. NEEDS CLARIFICATION contains one item: Tom said 'we should probably drop the video hero', met with 'mm-hm' — decision or musing?

The PM assigns the pricing page in the follow-up message and asks Tom to confirm the video hero in a one-line reply. Total elapsed time: four minutes. Both flagged items were exactly the ones that would have surfaced as surprises two weeks later.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, run the prompt on notes or a transcript from a real recent meeting. Count the UNASSIGNED and NEEDS CLARIFICATION items, verify one extracted decision against the source text, and send (or adapt) the follow-up message.
lessons.expectedResult: A structured record where decisions are backed by references, at least the genuinely ownerless actions are flagged rather than plausibly assigned, and a follow-up draft is ready in minutes instead of a quarter-hour of manual writing.
commonMistakes: Asking to 'summarize the meeting' — you get readable prose in which decisions, discussion, and speculation are indistinguishable.
Letting Claude infer owners from who spoke most about a topic; talking about work and committing to it are different things.
Skipping meeting context, so Claude cannot tell whether 'the launch' refers to the thing being decided or background noise.
Sending the follow-up without reading the NEEDS CLARIFICATION section — that section exists because those items need a human judgment call.
lessons.proTip: Run this in a Project with your team's roles and current project names in the custom instructions. Extraction improves noticeably when Claude already knows that 'Elena' is the design lead and 'Phoenix' is the migration project, not a city.

lessons.title: Create long-form content with an outline-first workflow
lessons.summary: Write reports, guides and articles by locking an outline before any prose exists, then drafting section by section — the workflow that keeps 3,000-word pieces coherent and on-message.
lessons.goal: Produce a coherent long-form piece by approving structure first, drafting in sections, and finishing with a whole-piece consistency pass.
lessons.whyItMatters: Asking Claude for '2,000 words on X' in one shot produces prose that starts strong and drifts: arguments repeat, the middle sags, and the conclusion answers a slightly different question than the introduction posed. Professional writers do not draft this way and neither should your AI workflow. Outline-first fixes it structurally — you correct the piece's argument when it is ten cheap bullet points, not two thousand expensive words — and section-by-section drafting keeps every part accountable to an approved plan. The final full-read pass then catches the seams that section work creates.
steps: Give Claude the brief: topic, audience, purpose (persuade, teach, document), target length, and the 2-3 points the piece must land.
Ask for an outline only — sections with a one-line summary of each section's job and rough word counts — and explicitly forbid prose at this stage.
Edit the outline like an editor: reorder, merge, cut, and check that each section advances the piece's core argument. This is the highest-leverage five minutes of the whole workflow.
Lock the outline, then request section 1 alone, telling Claude to stay within that section's job and not preview later sections' content.
Review each section before requesting the next; give corrections immediately, because approved sections become the standard the following ones match.
For fact-heavy sections, supply your source material and instruct Claude to use only those facts, marking anything it cannot support with [VERIFY].
After the last section, ask for a consistency pass over the full piece: tone drift, repeated points, contradictions between sections, and whether the intro's promise matches the conclusion.
Read the full piece yourself start to finish — the workflow reduces your editing burden; it does not remove your byline.
lessons.prompt:
I'm writing [CONTENT TYPE, e.g. "a practical guide"] titled "[WORKING TITLE]" for [AUDIENCE]. Purpose: [WHAT IT MUST ACHIEVE]. Target length: about [N] words.

It must land these points:
1. [KEY POINT 1]
2. [KEY POINT 2]
3. [KEY POINT 3]

STEP 1 — OUTLINE ONLY. Do not write any prose yet. Give me:
- A section-by-section outline with a heading, a one-line description of the section's job in the overall argument, and a target word count per section.
- One line on the through-line: how the piece gets from the opening to the conclusion.
- Any point above that you think is weakly supported or belongs in a different order — push back now, not mid-draft.

After I approve the outline, I'll request sections one at a time. When drafting: stay strictly within the approved section's scope, match [TONE, e.g. "plain, direct, first person plural"], and where you state a fact I haven't given you, mark it [VERIFY] rather than asserting it.
lessons.explanation: Separating outline approval from drafting converts structural editing from expensive to cheap — reordering bullets takes seconds; restructuring finished prose takes an hour and usually doesn't happen. Giving each section a stated 'job' does double duty: it forces the outline to be an argument rather than a topic list, and it becomes the scope constraint during drafting that stops sections from wandering into each other's territory. Inviting pushback at the outline stage exploits something real: Claude often spots a weak point or better ordering, but only volunteers it when asked. The [VERIFY] convention keeps drafting fast without letting unsourced claims masquerade as checked facts in the final piece.
lessons.example:
An SEO specialist writes a 2,500-word pillar guide, 'Technical SEO for E-commerce Migrations'. The outline comes back with seven sections — and a pushback note: the planned 'common mistakes' section overlaps two others and would read as repetition; Claude suggests distributing the mistakes into the relevant sections instead. She agrees, a fix that would have cost a full rewrite if discovered after drafting.

Sections are drafted one at a time; in section 4 she pastes her own crawl-data examples and the [VERIFY] rule flags two statistics Claude reached for that she hadn't supplied. The final consistency pass catches that sections 2 and 6 both explain redirect mapping, and trims the second occurrence to a cross-reference. Total drafting time: under an hour, and the piece reads like one author wrote it.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, produce a 1,200-2,000 word piece you actually need using the full workflow: brief with must-land points, outline-only with invited pushback, at least three sections drafted individually with your corrections between them, then a consistency pass. Note what the outline stage caught.
lessons.expectedResult: A finished long-form piece where every section audibly serves the argument, the consistency pass found at least one repetition or drift you'd have missed, and any [VERIFY] flags were resolved before you called it done.
commonMistakes: Skipping outline review because it 'looks fine' — the outline is where fixing structure costs seconds instead of rewrites.
Requesting all sections in one message after outline approval, which quietly recreates single-shot drafting and its drift.
Not correcting tone in early sections, then needing to fix the same drift in every later section that matched them.
Shipping without the consistency pass; section-by-section work is precisely what creates cross-section repetition, and only a whole-piece read catches it.
lessons.proTip: Before the outline, ask Claude for the three strongest objections your target audience would raise against the piece's main argument — then make sure the outline answers them. Long-form that pre-empts its readers' objections reads dramatically more authoritative.

lessons.title: Data analysis workflows: from raw CSV to an executive summary
lessons.summary: Upload a raw CSV to Claude, use its code-running analysis tool to profile, clean and analyze the data, and finish with charts and an executive summary a non-analyst can act on.
lessons.goal: Run a disciplined analysis pipeline on a real CSV — profile, clean, analyze, visualize — and produce an executive summary whose every number came from executed code.
lessons.whyItMatters: Claude's analysis tool writes and runs actual code against your uploaded files, which changes the trust model completely: numbers come from computation you can inspect, not from a language model's impression of your data. But a trustworthy result still requires an analyst's discipline — profiling before analyzing, handling data quality issues explicitly, and separating computed findings from interpretation. Professionals who follow that sequence turn hours of spreadsheet work into minutes; those who skip to 'find insights' get confident narratives built on unexamined data.
lessons.beforeYouStart: You need a real CSV (sales export, survey results, campaign data — a few hundred to a few hundred thousand rows) and a paid Claude plan with the analysis tool enabled in settings. Remove or anonymize sensitive personal data first.
steps: Upload the CSV and start with profiling only: row count, columns and types, missing values per column, duplicates, and the min/max/outliers of key numeric columns. No analysis yet.
Tell Claude what the data is and what decision the analysis serves — column names alone routinely mislead ('revenue' gross or net? 'date' order date or ship date?).
Review the profile and make data-quality decisions yourself: how to treat missing values, whether outliers are errors or your most important customers, which duplicates to drop.
State your analysis questions explicitly — 3-5 of them, tied to the decision — rather than asking Claude to 'find insights'.
Have Claude run the analysis with code and report which computations produced each result, so every figure is traceable.
Ask for 2-3 charts that answer your questions directly, each with a title stating its takeaway, not just its axes.
Request the executive summary: headline findings with numbers, what they mean for the decision, and a caveats section covering the data-quality choices made along the way.
Sanity-check one or two headline numbers against the raw file or your own quick calculation before circulating.
lessons.prompt:
I've uploaded [FILENAME]. It contains [WHAT THE DATA IS, e.g. "12 months of order data from our online store"]. Column notes: [CLARIFY AMBIGUOUS COLUMNS, e.g. "'revenue' is net of refunds; 'region' is shipping region"]. This analysis supports the decision: [DECISION, e.g. "where to focus Q4 marketing spend"].

PHASE 1 — PROFILE ONLY. Using code, report: row/column counts, data types, missing values per column, duplicate rows, and ranges/outliers for key numeric columns. Flag anything that looks like a data-quality problem. Do not analyze yet — wait for my instructions on handling the issues you find.

PHASE 2 — after I respond, answer these questions, computing everything with code:
1. [QUESTION 1, e.g. "Which product categories drive the most revenue and how has that mix shifted by quarter?"]
2. [QUESTION 2]
3. [QUESTION 3]

For each answer, state the computation behind it. Create one chart per question with a takeaway-stating title.

PHASE 3 — write an executive summary for [AUDIENCE, e.g. "our leadership team, non-technical"]: max one page, headline findings with the numbers, what each implies for [DECISION], and a 'Caveats' section listing data-quality issues and the handling choices we made. Do not include any number that did not come from the computed analysis.
lessons.explanation: The three-phase structure enforces the discipline that separates analysis from storytelling. Profiling first catches the problems — 8% missing regions, a duplicated export batch, a decimal-shifted outlier — that would otherwise silently corrupt every downstream number; pausing for your handling decisions matters because whether outliers are errors or VIP customers is business judgment, not a computation. Stating the computation behind each result keeps findings traceable to executed code, and the closing rule — no number outside the computed analysis — draws a hard line against the failure mode where a fluent summary quietly includes figures from nowhere. The caveats section makes the summary honest enough to survive a sharp question in the meeting where it's presented.
lessons.example:
An e-commerce owner uploads a year of orders to decide Q4 ad spend. Phase 1 finds 214 duplicate rows from a double export and reveals that 6% of orders have region 'UNKNOWN'. She decides: drop exact duplicates, keep UNKNOWN as its own segment.

Phase 2 computes that two categories produce 71% of net revenue, that the 'home' category doubled its share since spring, and — via the repeat-purchase question — that repeat customers have 2.3x the average order value. Each chart's title states its point ('Home category share doubled between Q1 and Q3'). The Phase 3 summary recommends concentrating Q4 spend on the two lead categories with a retention push, and its caveats note the dropped duplicates and the UNKNOWN-region segment. She checks the 71% figure with a pivot table — it matches — and sends the one-pager to her co-founder.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, upload a real CSV from your work (anonymized if needed) and run all three phases: profile, decide on at least one data-quality issue yourself, ask three decision-linked questions, and get the executive summary with caveats. Verify one headline number independently.
lessons.expectedResult: A profile that surfaced at least one issue worth a decision, computed answers with traceable calculations and takeaway-titled charts, and a one-page summary whose caveats section would survive scrutiny — with your spot-check matching.
commonMistakes: Opening with 'find interesting insights' — you get generic observations instead of answers to the questions your decision needs.
Skipping the profiling phase, then building the entire analysis on duplicates or misread columns.
Letting Claude silently choose how to handle missing values and outliers; those are business decisions that belong to you and to the caveats section.
Circulating the summary without one independent spot-check — traceable computation makes verification easy, which is exactly why skipping it is inexcusable.
lessons.proTip: After the analysis, ask: 'Which finding is most likely to be an artifact of a data-quality problem rather than a real effect? Re-run it with the alternative handling choice and tell me if the conclusion survives.' One-question robustness checks catch fragile findings before your audience does.

lessons.title: Use Claude memory and conversation strategy across a real project
lessons.summary: Manage Claude's memory, Projects, and chat boundaries deliberately so a weeks-long piece of work stays organized — and context lands where it persists instead of dying in old chats.
lessons.goal: Set up a deliberate system for a multi-week project: memory curated, durable context in Project instructions and knowledge, and one-chat-per-task working habits.
lessons.whyItMatters: Claude now has several kinds of persistence — memory that carries relevant context across chats (available to all users, with an editable summary in Settings), Projects with instructions and knowledge files, and the chats themselves — and professionals who don't manage them deliberately end up with the worst of both: a memory full of stale preferences, a 300-message mega-chat where early decisions are buried, and key project facts trapped in conversations nobody will reopen. A simple placement rule — durable facts in Project knowledge, personal preferences in memory, one task per chat — keeps a long-running project navigable for weeks.
steps: Open Claude's Settings and read your current memory summary. Edit out anything stale or wrong — this summary silently shapes future answers, so curating it is maintenance, not housekeeping.
Create a Project for the multi-week effort. Put durable facts — goals, stakeholders, constraints, deadlines, glossary — into the custom instructions and knowledge files, not into chat messages.
Adopt one-chat-per-task: 'draft the survey questions' is a chat; 'the project' is not. Small chats keep context sharp and make past work findable by title.

When a chat produces a durable decision or artifact, promote it: add the decision to the project instructions or upload the output to project knowledge. Chats are where work happens; the project is where results live.
Start each new task chat with a two-line pointer instead of a recap: what this chat is for and which project decisions constrain it.
Use incognito chats for explorations that shouldn't shape memory — half-baked ideas, sensitive topics, one-off tangents outside your normal patterns.
Do a weekly five-minute sweep: promote anything durable from the week's chats, delete dead-end threads, and re-check the memory summary.
lessons.prompt:
This chat is for one task: [TASK, e.g. "drafting the stakeholder survey for the rebrand project"].

Relevant project decisions that constrain this task (from our project knowledge): [2-3 POINTERS, e.g. "we're targeting existing customers only; tone decision from Aug 2 chat: 'evolution, not revolution'; deadline Aug 20"].

Stay scoped to this task. If you need background that isn't in this project's knowledge or instructions, ask rather than assuming.

At the end, when I say "wrap up", give me: (1) a 3-line summary of what we produced and decided here, phrased so I can paste it into the project's knowledge, and (2) anything from this chat that sounds like a durable decision I should promote to the project instructions.
lessons.explanation: This opener operationalizes the placement rule. The scoping line keeps the chat a task, not a junk drawer. The decision pointers give sharper context than a paragraph recap — and pointing at project knowledge rather than restating it means there is one authoritative version of each fact instead of drifting paraphrases. The 'ask rather than assuming' line covers the gap where needed background exists only in some other chat. The wrap-up ritual is the piece most people miss: it makes each chat produce its own promotion-ready summary, so moving results into durable storage costs one paste instead of an archaeology session through 60 messages three weeks later.
lessons.example:
A freelance brand consultant runs a six-week rebrand. Week 1: she creates the 'Rivera Rebrand' project — client background, brand direction decision, stakeholder list, deadlines in instructions; the signed brief in knowledge. She prunes her memory summary, deleting a stale note about a past client's preferences that had been coloring tone suggestions.

Weeks 2-5: each work item is its own chat — 'competitor positioning scan', 'tagline shortlist', 'stakeholder survey draft' — each opened with the two-line pointer, each ended with 'wrap up'. Promoted summaries accumulate in project knowledge. When the client asks in week 5 why direction B was dropped, she reopens the aptly titled 'direction shortlist' chat and answers with the actual reasoning in under a minute — while her colleague on a rival account scrolls a single 400-message thread looking for the same kind of answer.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account: read and prune your memory summary in Settings, create a Project for something real that will run multiple weeks, seed instructions and knowledge with the durable facts, then run two separate task chats using the opening prompt — ending each with 'wrap up' and actually promoting one result into the project.
lessons.expectedResult: A curated memory summary, a project whose knowledge holds the durable facts, and two findable task chats whose outcomes live in the project — so your next chat starts informed without any recap paragraph.
commonMistakes: Never reading the memory summary, then wondering why answers keep reflecting a preference from a project that ended months ago.
Running one endless mega-chat where week-old decisions are buried beyond retrieval and early context has long since stopped helping.
Pasting the same background into every new chat instead of putting it in project instructions once — re-typing what persistence should handle.
Letting decisions live only in the chat where they happened; if it matters next week, it belongs in project knowledge or instructions.
lessons.proTip: Keep a 'decision log' file in project knowledge — one line per decision with the date. It becomes the project's authoritative history, and pointing new chats at it beats any recap.

lessons.title: Quality control: verification passes, self-review prompts and fact-grounding
lessons.summary: Add a systematic verification layer to your Claude workflows: ground claims in supplied sources, run structured self-review passes, and know which checks only a human can make.
lessons.goal: Apply a three-layer quality-control routine — grounding rules at draft time, a structured self-review pass, and targeted human spot-checks — to any output that matters.
lessons.whyItMatters: The professionals who get burned by AI aren't the ones using it most — they're the ones shipping first drafts unreviewed. Claude's failure modes are quiet: a fluent paragraph containing an unsupported claim reads identically to one that's fully grounded. Quality control fixes this structurally rather than by vigilance: grounding instructions constrain what can enter a draft, a separate self-review pass catches what grounding missed (review works better as its own step than as an instruction inside the drafting prompt), and knowing the verification hierarchy tells you where your limited human checking time buys the most safety.
steps: At draft time, ground the work: supply source material and instruct Claude to use only facts from it, marking anything else [UNSUPPORTED]. Unverifiable-but-needed claims get [VERIFY], not silent inclusion.
Draft as normal. Do not pile review instructions into the drafting prompt — a generator grading itself mid-generation does both jobs worse.

Run a separate self-review pass with a specific checklist: unsupported factual claims, internal contradictions, ambiguities a hostile reader could exploit, and compliance with your original constraints.
Make the review adversarial by role: 'review this as the skeptical [CFO / opposing counsel / angry customer] who wants to find a problem' finds different issues than 'check this please'.
For each flagged issue, decide yourself: fix, verify externally, or accept with eyes open. Claude flags; you judge.
Spend human verification where model checking is weakest: exact numbers, names, dates, quotes, legal or financial assertions, and anything that commits you or your client to something.
For recurring output types, save the checklist as a reusable review prompt so quality stops depending on your memory on a deadline day.
lessons.prompt:
Review the draft below before I send it. Act as a skeptical [REVIEWER ROLE, e.g. "client CFO who will challenge anything imprecise"]. The source material it must stay grounded in is attached/pasted below the draft.

Run these checks separately and report findings under each heading:

1. GROUNDING — list every factual claim (numbers, dates, names, commitments) and mark each: SUPPORTED (quote the supporting line from the source), UNSUPPORTED (appears nowhere in the source), or CONTRADICTED (conflicts with the source — quote both sides).
2. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY — statements that contradict each other within the draft, including subtle ones like a total that doesn't match its parts.
3. RISKY AMBIGUITY — phrasings a hostile or literal-minded reader could interpret against my interests. Suggest tighter wording for each.
4. CONSTRAINT CHECK — my original requirements were: [LIST, e.g. "under 400 words, no pricing commitments, formal tone"]. Report compliance on each.

Rules: do not rewrite the draft. Do not soften findings to be agreeable — a missed problem costs me more than an awkward truth. If a section has no findings, say 'no findings' rather than inventing minor points to seem thorough.

DRAFT:
[PASTE DRAFT]

SOURCE MATERIAL:
[PASTE SOURCES]
lessons.explanation: Separating review from drafting matters because the checks are different cognitive jobs: generation optimizes for coherence, review for fault-finding, and a fresh pass with an adversarial role reliably surfaces problems the drafting pass smoothed over. The grounding section's claim-by-claim verdict with quoted evidence is the heart of it — it converts 'this looks right' into an auditable table, and CONTRADICTED as a distinct category catches the dangerous case where the draft says almost what the source says. 'Do not rewrite' keeps authority with you: Claude reports, you decide. The two honesty rules — don't soften, don't pad — counter the model's twin tendencies toward agreeableness and toward manufacturing findings to appear diligent.
lessons.example:
A lawyer drafts a settlement summary letter with Claude, grounded in the signed agreement, then runs the review prompt with 'opposing counsel looking for an opening' as the role.

GROUNDING flags one CONTRADICTED item: the draft says payment is due 'within 30 days of signature'; the agreement's clause 4.2 says 'within 30 days of the effective date' — quoted side by side. Different dates, real exposure. RISKY AMBIGUITY flags 'we consider this matter resolved' as broader than the agreement's actual release scope and suggests limiting language. CONSTRAINT CHECK confirms length and tone. The lawyer fixes both findings and independently re-reads clause 4.2 herself — the human check on the one claim that could have cost money. The letter goes out grounded, reviewed, and verified where it counted.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, take something real you drafted with Claude this week — an email, summary, or proposal section — plus its source material, and run the review prompt with a well-chosen adversarial role. Triage every finding as fix, verify, or accept, and perform one human verification on the highest-stakes claim.
lessons.expectedResult: A claim-by-claim grounding table with at least one finding worth acting on, sharper wording for any risky ambiguities, and the experience of catching an issue before your reader did — in about three minutes of review.
commonMistakes: Bundling 'and double-check everything' into the drafting prompt and calling that review — a dedicated pass with a checklist finds substantially more.
Accepting 'looks good overall' as a review; without required categories and per-claim verdicts, you get reassurance, not scrutiny.
Treating a clean self-review as final verification for high-stakes claims — the review tells you where to look; exact numbers, dates, and legal commitments still need a human check.
Skipping quality control on 'routine' output — the unreviewed Tuesday email, not the big proposal, is where the wrong date usually ships.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running list of every real error your reviews catch. After a month, fold the recurring types into your drafting prompts as standing rules — the best quality-control system is the one that stops making its most common mistakes upstream.

lessons.title: Combine Claude web, desktop, mobile and Chrome into one workflow
lessons.summary: Stop treating Claude's surfaces as separate apps: route each part of your day to the right one — mobile for capture, web and desktop for deep work, Claude in Chrome for browser tasks — with Projects as the connective tissue.
lessons.goal: Design and run a personal cross-surface workflow where capture, deep work, and in-browser action each happen on the best surface, connected by shared Projects and memory.
lessons.whyItMatters: Claude runs on the web (claude.ai), as desktop apps for macOS and Windows, on iOS and Android, and inside your browser via the Claude in Chrome extension (open beta on all paid plans as of August 2026). Your account, Projects, memory, and chat history sync across all of them — which means the question is no longer 'where is Claude?' but 'which surface fits this moment?'. Professionals who route deliberately capture ideas the moment they occur, do document-heavy work where files and screen space live, and let Chrome handle the web tasks that used to mean twenty minutes of tab-juggling — without ever rebuilding context, because it travels with the account.
lessons.beforeYouStart: You need a paid Claude plan for Claude in Chrome (no free tier; Chrome only). Install the mobile app and the Chrome extension, and sign into the same account everywhere.
steps: Map your Claude moments for a typical week into three buckets: capture (ideas, quick questions, on the move), deep work (documents, analysis, drafting), and browser work (research across sites, forms, web apps).

Route capture to mobile: start project-related thoughts as chats inside the relevant Project so they're waiting in context when you sit down — voice input makes this viable while walking out of a meeting.
Route deep work to desktop or web, where file uploads, Artifacts, the analysis tool, and screen space live. Pick up your mobile capture chats here and develop them.
Set up Claude in Chrome: review its site-level permissions and grant access deliberately, starting with the handful of sites where browser help pays off most.

Use Chrome for genuinely browser-shaped tasks — comparing options across several open tabs, summarizing a long page in place, filling a form from reference info — and keep reviewing anything it does before submission.

Practice Chrome hygiene: keep tabs with sensitive accounts (banking, health, admin consoles) out of sessions where Claude is active, and treat instructions embedded in web pages as untrusted — prompt injection via malicious page content is the documented risk.
Close the loop: promote anything durable a mobile or Chrome session produced into the relevant Project, so every surface deposits into the same shared context.
After a week, audit the routing: anything you did on an awkward surface out of habit becomes next week's routing fix.
lessons.prompt:
I want to design my cross-surface Claude workflow. Here is my typical working week: [DESCRIBE: e.g. "mornings writing client proposals at my desk, afternoons in meetings and site visits, lots of supplier research across websites, ideas arrive while commuting"].

I use: Claude on desktop/web, the mobile app, and Claude in Chrome. All on one account with shared Projects and memory.

Design my routing:
1. For each recurring activity above, name the best surface and the concrete habit — e.g. "supplier research → Chrome: have Claude compare the open tabs and log the comparison to the Suppliers project".
2. Identify handoffs: where work starts on one surface and continues on another, and how to make each handoff seamless using Projects (what to capture, where it should land, how to pick it up).
3. For Claude in Chrome specifically: given my activities, which sites should I grant permissions to, and which of my tasks should NOT go through the browser for safety or reliability reasons?
4. Give me a one-week trial plan: which two habits to build first, and what would tell me the routing is working.

Be concrete and opinionated. If an activity fits badly on every surface, say so rather than forcing an answer.
lessons.explanation: This prompt works because it makes Claude design around your actual week instead of listing features — routing is only useful when it attaches surfaces to recurring real activities. The handoff question targets where cross-surface workflows genuinely break: not in any single app, but in the seams, which Projects exist to bridge. Asking which tasks should not go through Chrome bakes the safety judgment into the design phase — the permission model and the prompt-injection risk mean 'can' and 'should' differ, and it's better to decide that calmly up front than ad hoc with a form half-filled. Limiting the trial to two habits respects how routing actually sticks: one habit at a time, verified by a week of use, beats a grand system abandoned by Thursday.
lessons.example:
A real estate agent runs the prompt with her week: morning listing write-ups, afternoons of viewings, evenings comparing listings across portal sites. The routing comes back: viewing debriefs → mobile voice capture into the 'Active Listings' project within minutes of leaving each property; listing write-ups → desktop, where her write-up chat opens against the fresh viewing notes already sitting in the project; portal comparison → Claude in Chrome across her open tabs, with the comparison table saved back to the project.

For safety, the plan grants Chrome permissions to the two portal sites only, and explicitly keeps her transaction-management system out of Claude-active sessions. Her two trial habits: voice-capture after every viewing, and the Chrome comparison on Thursday evenings. By week's end, Thursday's portal session takes 25 minutes instead of 90, and her write-ups quote details from debriefs she'd previously have half-remembered.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, run the routing prompt with your real week. Implement the two trial habits it recommends — one must involve a handoff between surfaces through a Project — and configure Claude in Chrome's site permissions according to the safety split it proposed.
lessons.expectedResult: A written routing you actually follow for a week: at least one capture-to-desktop handoff that worked without re-explaining context, one browser task measurably faster in Chrome, and site permissions that reflect a deliberate safety decision.
commonMistakes: Using whichever surface is nearest for everything, then concluding cross-surface work 'doesn't click' — routing is a decision, not a default.
Capturing mobile thoughts in standalone chats outside any Project, so desktop sessions start from zero and the handoff value evaporates.
Granting Claude in Chrome broad site permissions on day one instead of starting narrow and expanding as trust builds.
Leaving sensitive logged-in tabs open during Chrome sessions — the documented prompt-injection risk means page content can carry hostile instructions, so separation is the discipline that matters.
lessons.proTip: Claude in Chrome can record a workflow so Claude learns the steps. Record your most repetitive browser chore once — a weekly report pulled from the same web app, a standard form — and it becomes a repeatable routine instead of a fresh explanation every time.
